title: Effective Field Theories for Material Media
authors: Angelo Esposito, Alberto Nicolis, Riccardo Penco
abstract: We review recent progress in understanding certain aspects of condensed matter systems from a high energy theory perspective. We discuss effective field theories that describe collective bulk and localized excitations in a variety of solid and fluid systems. Particular emphasis is placed on the role played by spacetime symmetries and their spontaneous breaking. The resulting Goldstone dynamics can be seen as underlying a wide variety of phenomena. We attempt to bridge the language gap between subfields while underscoring the numerous conceptual similarities.
summary: This review unifies the study of condensed matter physics by applying tools from high-energy field theory, specifically Effective Field Theories. It demonstrates that collective excitations in solids, fluids, and superfluids are often described by Goldstone bosons resulting from spontaneously broken symmetries. The work aims to bridge conceptual gaps between particle physics and material science using a systematic theoretical framework.
main_problem: The paper reviews how high-energy field theory concepts, particularly Effective Field Theories (EFTs) and symmetry breaking, can be used to systematically describe the low-energy dynamics of various condensed matter systems.
main_result: It argues that many phenomena in solids, fluids, and superfluids are governed by gapless Goldstone excitations arising from spontaneously broken symmetries, unifying language across subfields.
method: The primary method is theoretical review, employing EFT techniques to analyze collective excitations (like phonons) in different media while comparing results derived under relativistic versus nonrelativistic approximations.
model_or_system: The scope covers general condensed matter systems, including solids, fluids, and superfluids. The analysis focuses on the medium's ground state properties defined by broken spacetime symmetries, such as Lorentz boosts.
key_observables: Goldstone boson spectra, phonon scattering rates, superfluid dynamics (e.g., Hall viscosity), and low-energy excitation modes.
important_parameters: Low energy/long distance limit ($\vec{k} 	o 0$), temperature, density, and the nature of broken symmetries (e.g., boost invariance).
main_assumptions: The approach assumes that the low-energy physics can be captured by an EFT derived from underlying microscopic interactions; it often treats systems as being in a state where certain spacetime symmetries are spontaneously broken.
paper_structure: The paper is structured systematically by medium: Solids (Section 3), Fluids (Section 4), and Superfluids (Section 5), providing specialized derivations for each class of matter.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful, unifying theoretical lens—the EFT framework—to analyze many-body dynamics in condensed matter systems, drawing direct parallels between particle physics symmetry breaking and macroscopic material properties like sound propagation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The equilibrium configuration (dashed line) of a string in two spatial dimensions spontaneously breaks three symmetries: boosts along y, translations along y and rotations in the xy-plane. A given perturbation (solid line) can be seen as generated by the action of locally modulated translations along y (left panel), locally modulated rotations in the xy-plane (right panel) or locally modulated boosts (not shown). As a consequence, despite the breaking of these three symmetries, the perturbation can be described by a single Goldstone mode, δy(x), corresponding to the vertical displacement of the string.
Figure 2: Left panel: Relation between physical and comoving coordinates for a solid at equilibrium, Eq. (3.2). Right panel: Same relation but for a solid slightly away from equilibrium, Eq. (3.34).

Figure 3: Measured spectrum of collective modes in superfluid 4He, as report in [223]. In particular, blues circles are taken from [224], red triangles from [225], green diamonds from [226], and purple squares from [227]. The phonon region corresponds to the lowest momentum one, k ≲ΛUV ≃1.5 keV, where the lowest order linear dispersion relation is also plotted.

Figure 4: Parametrization of the vortex line configuration, Xµ(t, σ), in the τ = X0 = t gauge. Every slice with τ = fixed represents a spatial configuration of the string at a given instant in time. Every σ = fixed slice, instead, follows the motion of a given infinitesimal chunk of string through time.

Figure 5: Experimental image of a vortex lattice featuring a Tkachenko mode (black lines), as reported in [262]. The two panels correspond to the same lattice, imaged a two different instant of times after the excitation of the mode.
